ai.definition: Orbital satellites are spacecraft designed to orbit the Earth or other celestial bodies. They can be used for a variety of applications such as communication, navigation, weather monitoring, and military surveillance.
ai.howItWorks: Satellites operate by using onboard equipment like antennas, sensors, and computers to receive, process, and transmit data. They are launched into space on rockets and maintain their orbit through the use of propulsion systems or gravitational forces. Ground stations communicate with satellites for data transmission and control purposes.
ai.problemSolved: Orbital satellites solve the problem of providing global coverage for various applications that require real-time or near-real-time information, such as communication services, weather forecasting, and remote sensing.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves designing the satellite components, integrating them into a spacecraft, testing its functionality, and preparing it for launch. Materials like aluminum, titanium, and composite structures are commonly used due to their lightweight and durability properties.
ai.buildProcess: Satellites are built in clean rooms under controlled conditions. They undergo rigorous testing including thermal vacuum tests, vibration tests, and electromagnetic compatibility tests before being integrated into a launch vehicle.
ai.costDrivers: The primary cost drivers for orbital satellites include the development costs of the satellite itself (including R&D, design, and manufacturing), launch services, insurance, and operational costs such as ground station maintenance and data processing.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for orbital satellites is positive due to increasing demand from various sectors like telecommunications, government agencies, and private companies. However, there are challenges related to space debris management and regulatory compliance that need to be addressed.
ai.regulation: Orbital satellite operations are regulated by international bodies such as the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA) and regional entities like the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in the U.S. Regulations cover aspects like frequency allocation, orbit allocation, and debris mitigation.
ai.risks: Risks associated with orbital satellites include launch failure, operational failures, space debris collisions, and regulatory non-compliance. Additionally, there are environmental risks related to satellite end-of-life disposal and potential impacts on Earth's environment.
ai.profitability: The profitability of the orbital satellite industry varies depending on the application and market segment. Commercial communication satellites have a higher profit margin compared to government or military applications due to lower development costs and higher revenue streams from subscription services.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments in orbital satellites include miniaturization, increased use of electric propulsion systems for longer operational lifetimes, and the integration of artificial intelligence for enhanced data processing capabilities. There is also a growing interest in constellations of small satellites to provide global coverage with reduced costs.

subsystems.name: Payload
subsystems.role: the mission equipment that does the actual work — imaging, communications, sensing or science.

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: the platform that keeps the payload alive and pointed correctly.

subsystems.name: Attitude and orbit control
subsystems.role: knows where the satellite is pointing and keeps it stable.

subsystems.name: Propulsion
subsystems.role: changes orbit, maintains position and eventually deorbits.

subsystems.name: Communications
subsystems.role: links the satellite to the ground for commands and data.

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: the control centres and stations that fly the satellite and receive its data.

buildSteps.title: Define the mission and orbit
buildSteps.detail: Decide what the satellite must do — for example, image a region daily or relay signals — and choose an orbit: low Earth orbit for close views, geostationary for fixed coverage.

buildSteps.title: Design the satellite
buildSteps.detail: Engineers split the design into bus and payload, and set budgets for mass, electrical power, data rate and thermal load.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture components
buildSteps.detail: Solar cells, batteries, reaction wheels, instruments and radios are built and qualified for the vacuum, radiation and temperature swings of space.

buildSteps.title: Assemble and integrate
buildSteps.detail: The bus structure is built, harnesses are laid, and the payload is mounted and connected to power and data systems.

buildSteps.title: Test for launch and space
buildSteps.detail: The satellite is shaken on vibration tables, baked in thermal vacuum chambers and checked for electromagnetic interference to catch faults before launch.

buildSteps.title: Launch
buildSteps.detail: The satellite is packed into a fairing and carried by a rocket, either on a dedicated launch or as a rideshare with other spacecraft.

buildSteps.title: Commission in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Solar arrays and antennas deploy, systems are switched on, and the satellite is checked out before routine operation begins.

buildSteps.title: Operate for years
buildSteps.detail: Ground stations send commands, receive data, monitor health, and plan end-of-life disposal or deorbit.

prerequisites.why: without a rocket that can reach the intended orbit, the satellite never leaves the ground.
components must survive vacuum, radiation and temperature cycling that would destroy ordinary hardware.
satellites rely on sunlight for power and batteries for eclipse periods.
a satellite is useless without a way to send it commands and receive its data.
falling launch prices have widened access to orbit, but costs remain high for dedicated missions.

pathway.milestone: large constellations of small satellites in low Earth orbit for broadband and frequent imaging
pathway.unlocks: global connectivity and near-daily revisit of any point on Earth.

pathway.milestone: further reuse and mass production of satellites
pathway.unlocks: more affordable access and faster replacement of ageing spacecraft.

pathway.milestone: on-orbit servicing, refuelling and debris removal
pathway.unlocks: longer satellite lifetimes and less orbital congestion.

pathway.milestone: in-space assembly and manufacturing of large structures
pathway.unlocks: antennas and platforms far bigger than any rocket fairing can carry.
